Ancient Greece. The civilizations of the Greek-speaking peoples from roughly the eighth century BCE until the conquest by Rome in the second century BCE. Centered on the Aegean Sea and Mediterranean, ancient Greece was not a unified nation but a collection of independent city-states, or poleis, dominated by Athens and Sparta. Ancient Greece created the foundations of Western philosophy, democracy, drama, science, mathematics, architecture, and athletics.

Ancient Greek civilization emerged from the collapse of the Bronze Age Mycenaean civilization around eleven hundred BCE, followed by the Dark Ages from eleven hundred to eight hundred BCE. The Archaic Period from eight hundred to four hundred eighty BCE saw the rise of independent city-states. The Aegean Sea was central to Greek life: its islands and coast facilitated trade, communication, and colonization. Greeks established settlements throughout the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions, spreading Greek language and culture. Athens and Sparta emerged as the dominant city-states. Athens developed democracy, the first large-scale system of popular self-governance, while Sparta created a militaristic oligarchic state based on a warrior aristocracy.

The Greco-Persian Wars from four hundred ninety-five to four hundred seventy-nine BCE saw Greek city-states unite against Persian invasion. Athens defeated the Persian navy at Marathon in four hundred ninety BCE and Salamis in four hundred eighty BCE, establishing Athens as a major power. The Classical Period from four hundred eighty to three hundred twenty-three BCE witnessed Athens' golden age under Pericles: the construction of the Parthenon, the flowering of drama through playwrights like Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes, and philosophy through Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

Greek philosophy established traditions of rational inquiry. The Stoics, Epicureans, Cynics, and Skeptics debated fundamental questions of knowledge, ethics, and the good life. Greek democracy in Athens created the world's first system of citizenship and popular participation in governance, though it excluded women, slaves who comprised thirty percent of the population, and non-native residents. The Olympic Games, held every four years at Olympia, were a pan-Hellenic festival celebrating athletic excellence and divine favor, featuring competition in wrestling, boxing, running, discus, javelin, and other sports. Alexander the Great, the Macedonian conqueror from three hundred fifty-six to three hundred twenty-three BCE, conquered the Persian Empire and extended Greek civilization across Asia, ushering in the Hellenistic Era, which blended Greek and Oriental culture. Greek drama—tragedy and comedy—was performed at festivals like the City Dionysia and Lenaea and explored universal human themes of fate, justice, ambition, and the divine.
